title: How to build credit from scratch
summary: Learn the best ways to build your credit score. Explore proven methods for building credit and securing your financial health with Intuit.

- How to build credit from scratch


Building credit from scratch comes down to two things: getting at least one account reported to the credit bureaus, and giving it time. You generally won’t have a FICO Score until an account has been open at least six months and reported in the past six months, so your first half year is about setting up habits that show up on your report.


Whether you’re turning 18, have paid cash your whole life, or just moved to the U.S., the steps are mostly the same. This guide covers how long it takes, six ways to start, what doesn’t count and how to adjust the plan for your situation. Let’s start with why the timing matters.


## Key takeaways


- To get a FICO Score, you need at least one account open for six months or more and at least one account reported to a credit bureau in the past six months.
- A secured credit card, a credit-builder loan and becoming an authorized user are common ways to start. Debit cards, prepaid cards and payday loans generally don’t build credit history.
- Payment history is the biggest factor in a FICO Score, at about 35%. Amounts owed, which includes credit utilization, makes up about 30%.
- You don’t need to carry a balance to build credit. Paying your balance in full each month helps get you the best scores, according to the CFPB.
- You can get free credit reports from Equifax, Experian and TransUnion every week at AnnualCreditReport.com, and checking your own report doesn’t hurt your score.


## The importance of learning how to build credit early


The earlier you start using credit responsibly, the more time your credit history has to grow. Length of credit history makes up about 15% of a FICO Score,[according to FICO](https://www.myfico.com/credit-education/whats-in-your-credit-score) . A long, positive credit history demonstrates to lenders that you can manage debt reliably over time.


Good credit helps with milestones like buying a car, renting an apartment and applying for a mortgage. Many employers also look at credit reports as part of a background check,[according to the CFPB](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/could-i-be-turned-down-for-a-job-because-of-something-in-my-credit-report-en-1345/) . Building good credit also opens doors to better loan terms and lower interest rates.


How early you can start depends on your age. Under 18, being added as an authorized user on a parent’s card is usually the only route. At 18 you can apply for your own card, but until you turn 21, issuers generally need you to show an independent ability to pay or have a cosigner over 21,[according to the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/can-a-card-issuer-consider-my-age-when-deciding-whether-to-issue-a-credit-card-to-me-en-20/) .


Credit can matter later in ways you might not expect, too. If you start a business someday, credit cards are the number one source of financing for small businesses in the US, according to the[Intuit QuickBooks Small Business Index Annual Report 2025](https://quickbooks.intuit.com/r/small-business-data/index-annual-report-2025/) . The same report found that 55% of US small businesses charge more than 25% of all expenses to credit cards. Shanna Watkins, a co-founder of the non-alcoholic beverage company Sensori, didn’t have capital saved to start the business. What she had was strong credit, so she planned to use a line of credit as the initial capital.


> “I had taken care of my credit for you know, years and years and built that up to where I had a really good credit score.”
>
>
> Shanna Watkins, co-founder of Sensori, on[Resilience and Reinvention](https://omny.fm/shows/mind-the-business-small-business-success-stories/resilience-and-reinvention) , Mind the Business


But don’t stress if you didn’t start building credit as early as you could. There’s still time to start your credit journey and build up your score.


## How long does it take to build credit?


Expect about six months before you have a FICO Score. To be scored, you need at least one account open for six months or more and at least one account reported in the past six months,[according to myFICO](https://www.myfico.com/credit-education/credit-scores/how-to-build-credit) .[VantageScore models can score people whose accounts are less than six months old](https://www.vantagescore.com/why-vantagescore/financial-inclusion) , so you may see one of those sooner. After that, steady on-time payments are what move you toward[a good credit score](https://www.intuit.com/blog/innovative-thinking/financial-tips/good-credit-score/) .


Here’s what those first months can look like, with the one thing to do at each stage.


When What to do What shows up on your report Mistake to avoid


Month 0 Check your free reports at AnnualCreditReport.com, then open one starter account, such as a secured card, a student card or a credit-builder loan A new account, and usually a hard inquiry Applying for several accounts at once


Months 1 to 5 Put one bill you already pay on the card, and set autopay to pay the statement balance in full by the due date An on-time payment each month the lender reports Carrying a balance or missing a due date


Month 6 Check whether you have a FICO Score yet Enough history for a first FICO Score, if your account has been reporting Closing the account once the score appears


Months 7 to 12 Keep paying in full, and add a second account only if you need one A longer record of on-time payments Opening a loan you don’t need just to add to your credit mix


Say you open a secured card with a $500 deposit, which usually becomes your credit limit. You put your $40 phone bill on it each month and let autopay clear the statement balance. If your card has a grace period, you pay no interest on those purchases, your report shows six on-time payments by month six, and you have the history a FICO Score needs.


## 6 ways to start building credit


You only need one account reporting on time to get going, and most people start with one of the first three options below.


### 1. Open a credit card


Opening and using a credit card is one of the most common ways to build credit. But there are a couple of different types of cards you can choose from, some of which are designed for those who don’t have a credit score yet:


- Secured credit cards: These cards are designed specifically for people starting to build their credit. To open a secured credit card, you must submit a security deposit to the issuer upfront. This deposit is collateral if you don’t pay your bill and typically represents your credit limit. You’ll use it like a regular credit card, and you’ll be charged interest on any balance you don’t pay in full.
- Student credit cards: If you’re currently enrolled in college, student credit cards can be a good option to start building credit. These cards are designed with students in mind and often have lower credit requirements than traditional cards. Some offer perks like cash back or rewards, depending on the issuer.
- Retail credit cards: Department stores or specific brands offer these cards. They’re often easier to qualify for than other types of credit cards, even if you have limited or no credit history. Many work only at the affiliated store or brand and often come with low credit limits, and their discounts can tempt you to overspend.


Before you apply, confirm the card reports to all three credit bureaus. If you’re not sure where to start, the bank or credit union where you already have a checking account is a reasonable first stop.


### 2. Become an authorized user


Becoming an authorized user on a parent’s credit card (assuming they have good credit and the card issuer reports authorized users) can be a great way to start building credit at a young age. When you’re an authorized user, you can receive a credit card in your name that’s connected to your parent’s account.


As the primary cardholder practices responsible credit habits like making on-time payments and keeping a low credit card balance, their positive credit behavior will reflect on your credit report and help you build a strong foundation.


It’s important to remember that irresponsible habits by the primary cardholder, such as missed payments or maxing out the card, could also impact your credit as an authorized user. Before becoming one, clearly discuss expectations for using the card responsibly with the primary cardholder.


There are limits to know about. Card issuers[aren’t required to report authorized users](https://www.experian.com/blogs/ask-experian/are-authorized-user-accounts-reported-to-all-three-bureaus/) , and some won’t report a child until they turn 18. Being an authorized user also doesn’t have as big of an impact on your own score as an account in your name, according to myFICO. While becoming an authorized user can help you kick-start your credit, consider opening your own credit card account once you have a foundational score to establish credit more effectively and boost your score faster.


### 3. Get a loan


A loan can help build credit when it’s one you’d take out anyway. Choose one that fits your needs and budget, and make every payment on time. Here are some loan options that can help you build credit:


- Student loans: If you’re enrolled in college, student loans can help cover tuition and other expenses while contributing to your credit history. Make payments on time to show your ability to manage debt responsibly.
- Auto loans: Buying a car with an auto loan can be a good way to build credit, especially if you have a down payment and can afford the monthly payments. Regular, timely payments on an auto loan can positively impact your credit score.
- Secured loans: These loans are[backed by collateral](https://www.experian.com/blogs/ask-experian/what-is-a-secured-loan/) , such as a savings account or certificate of deposit. This lowers the lender’s risk, which may make them easier to qualify for even with a limited credit history.
- Credit-builder loans: These loans are designed for building credit. Instead of getting the money upfront, the lender holds it in a savings account while you make payments, usually over six to 24 months,[according to the CFPB](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/what-are-some-ways-to-start-or-rebuild-a-good-credit-history-en-2155/) . When you finish, you get the money back, and your on-time payments show up on your credit report. These loans typically range from about $300 to $1,000,[according to Credit Karma](https://www.creditkarma.com/personal-loans/i/credit-builder-loan) , which suggests confirming the lender reports to all three bureaus.


Some credit-builder products charge a monthly fee. Compare that cost with a secured card that has no annual fee before you sign up, and keep any credit-builder account current, since a missed payment gets reported too.


### 4. Use a cosigner


Using a cosigner, someone who agrees to share legal responsibility for the debt with you, can improve your chances of loan approval, especially if you have no credit history, a low credit score, or lower income.


A cosigner with good credit can help you qualify for better loan terms. Also, having a cosigned loan and making timely payments can help you build or improve your credit history, as the account will appear on your credit report.


However, using a cosigner comes with some risks and extra responsibilities. Both you and the cosigner are equally responsible for repaying the loan, meaning that if you fail to make payments, the cosigner must legally cover them. This shared responsibility can put pressure on personal relationships and negatively impact both parties’ credit scores if payments are missed. Late or missed payments on a cosigned loan[can appear on both credit reports](https://www.experian.com/blogs/ask-experian/how-does-cosigning-affect-your-credit/) , damage your credit and can significantly harm the cosigner’s credit score, making it harder for them to borrow in the future.


Before asking someone to be a cosigner, discuss your repayment plan, financial responsibilities, and the potential risks for both of you.


### 5. Build a credit mix over time


Credit mix is the variety of accounts on your report, such as revolving credit like credit cards and installment loans like auto and student loans. It makes up about 10% of a FICO Score, and[myFICO says](https://www.myfico.com/credit-education/whats-in-your-credit-score) it’s not necessary to have one of each.


Mix counts for more when your report doesn’t have much other information on it, which is often the case when you’re starting out. That still isn’t a reason to borrow money you don’t need. Let your mix grow as you take on credit for real needs, and space out your applications.


### 6. Learn good credit habits


Creating good credit habits is the foundation of building and maintaining a strong credit score. Here are a few tips on how to establish those habits.


#### Prioritize on-time payments


Consistently paying your bills on or before the due date is one of the most important factors in building good credit. Your payment history accounts for roughly 35% of your FICO score, so even a few late payments can significantly pull it down. Utilize automatic payments, calendar alerts, or reminder apps to keep due dates front and center, ensuring timely bill payments every time.


#### Pay your statement balance in full


Each card statement shows what you owe for that billing period and a due date. If your card has a[grace period](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/what-is-a-grace-period-for-a-credit-card-en-47/) , paying the full statement balance by the due date every month lets you avoid interest on new purchases. Cash advances usually start charging interest right away. And[you don’t need to carry a balance](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/how-do-i-get-and-keep-a-good-credit-score-en-318/) to get a good score, the CFPB says.


#### Maintain a low credit utilization ratio


Credit utilization is the amount of credit you use compared to your available credit. It falls under amounts owed, which makes up about 30% of a FICO Score. Experts advise using no more than 30% of your total credit limit, according to the CFPB. With a $1,000 limit, that means a balance of $300 or less, and lower is better.


#### Monitor your credit reports


You can get free reports from Equifax, Experian and TransUnion every week at[AnnualCreditReport.com](https://www.annualcreditreport.com/) , and checking your own report doesn’t hurt your score. You can also check your TransUnion and Equifax reports for free with[Credit Karma](https://www.creditkarma.com/free-credit-report) . Look for errors, accounts you don’t recognize and signs of identity theft, and dispute anything that’s wrong with the credit bureau.


#### Apply for new credit sparingly


Most credit applications trigger a hard inquiry on your credit report. For most people, one more inquiry takes less than five points off a FICO Score, and inquiries only affect the score for a year,[according to myFICO](https://www.myfico.com/credit-education/credit-reports/credit-checks-and-inquiries) . Apply only when you need credit and are likely to be approved.


#### Don’t close existing credit cards or accounts


Keeping older accounts open, especially ones with no annual fee, preserves your available credit. Closing a card can raise your utilization and lower your score. If you keep a card you rarely use, check it now and then so a forgotten charge doesn’t turn into a late payment.


## What doesn’t build credit


Some everyday money habits never reach your credit report.[According to the CFPB](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/what-are-some-ways-to-start-or-rebuild-a-good-credit-history-en-2155/) , these generally don’t help you build credit history:


- Debit cards and cash
- Prepaid cards
- Payday loans
- “Buy here, pay here” auto loans


A typical debit card doesn’t build credit because it draws on money already in your bank account. A few newer cards marketed as debit cards do report to the credit bureaus, but they’re usually tied to a line of credit,[according to Credit Karma](https://www.creditkarma.com/money/i/does-debit-card-build-credit) .


Rent and utility bills usually aren’t on your report either. Most landlords don’t report rent, so you may need to sign up with a rent-reporting service to get on-time payments on your credit report,[Credit Karma notes](https://www.creditkarma.com/credit/i/how-to-build-credit-from-scratch) . Most utility companies don’t report on-time payments, though an unpaid bill sent to collections can appear, the CFPB says.[Experian Boost](https://www.experian.com/consumer-products/score-boost.html) lets you add eligible on-time bills, like phone, utility and streaming payments, to your Experian credit file for free, but it only affects scores based on Experian data.


## How to build credit in your situation


The basics stay the same for everyone, but where you start changes the first step.


### If you’re 18 to 20


An 18-year-old community college student with a minimum-wage job posted on Reddit’s r/personalfinance after getting a first card with a $1,000 limit. Their mom said to keep a small balance on it to build credit, which conflicted with what they’d read. Commenters said to pay it off in full. You don’t need to carry a balance to build credit.


At your age, a student card or a secured card is the usual first step, and you’ll need to show an independent ability to pay or have a cosigner over 21. If a parent adds you as an authorized user, open your own account too, since that’s what lenders weigh most.[Financial literacy for college students](https://www.intuit.com/blog/innovative-thinking/financial-tips/financial-literacy-college-students/) covers more money habits worth starting now.


### If you’ve always paid with cash or debit


A 43-year-old in Reddit’s r/CreditCards wrote that for about 15 years they’d paid for everything in cash or with a debit card, had no recent payment history, and didn’t know where to begin. That’s a common spot, because typical debit card purchases don’t show up on a credit report.


Start with the bank or credit union you already use and ask about a secured card. Move one recurring bill onto it, pay the statement in full and give it six months. You can also add bills you already pay to your Experian file with Experian Boost while your new account builds history.


### If you’re new to the U.S.


An international student on Reddit’s r/CreditCards described being turned down by several issuers, including for secured cards, while applying with an Individual Taxpayer Identification Number. Each application can add a hard inquiry, so apply where you’re likely to qualify.


Some major card issuers accept an ITIN in place of a Social Security number,[according to Experian](https://www.experian.com/blogs/ask-experian/how-to-apply-for-credit-card-without-social-security-number/) . Ask the bank where you have an account first, and if your spouse or partner has good credit, becoming an authorized user on their card can give you a head start.


### If you’re a parent helping a teen


One parent on Reddit’s r/personalfinance said they and their spouse had added their son as an authorized user on cards dating back to 2003, and he turned 18 with a 763 score. The most upvoted reply said to let him pick his own card, and that his score wouldn’t climb much higher for a while because of his age of credit.


Before you add your teen, ask your card issuer whether it reports authorized users and at what age. Your late payments would show up on their report too. When they turn 18, help them pick a first card of their own.[Financial literacy for teens and young adults](https://www.intuit.com/blog/innovative-thinking/financial-tips/financial-literacy-teens-young-adults/) has ideas for the conversations that go with it.


## Build and track your credit with Credit Karma


Intuit Credit Karma gives you free VantageScore 3.0 credit scores from Equifax and TransUnion, so you can watch your new score appear and grow. Credit Karma’s[Credit Builder](https://www.creditkarma.com/credit-builder) plan pairs a line of credit with a locked savings account and reports your payments to all three credit bureaus, so you can build credit while you save. Banking services are provided by Cross River Bank, Member FDIC.[Create a free Credit Karma account](https://www.creditkarma.com/signup) to start tracking your progress, and see[what goes into a credit score](https://www.intuit.com/blog/innovative-thinking/what-is-credit-score/) as yours takes shape.

## Frequently asked questions about building credit


### Does checking my credit hurt my score?


No. Checking your own credit report[has no effect on your score](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/will-requesting-my-credit-report-hurt-my-credit-score-en-1229/) , according to the CFPB. Hard inquiries happen when a lender checks your credit after you apply. For more on where to look, see[how to check your credit score](https://www.intuit.com/blog/innovative-thinking/financial-tips/check-credit-score/) .


### Do rent payments build credit?


Only if they’re reported to a credit bureau and the score being used counts them. Landlords reporting rent isn’t common practice, according to myFICO. Newer models like FICO 10T and VantageScore 4.0 take rent payment history into account,[according to the Federal Housing Finance Agency](https://www.fhfa.gov/policy/credit-scores) .


### Does buy now, pay later build credit?


Usually not.[Most buy now, pay later providers don’t report to the credit bureaus](https://www.experian.com/blogs/ask-experian/what-is-buy-now-pay-later-and-does-it-impact-my-credit/) , according to Experian. If yours does report, the plan can show up on your report, and late or missed payments can affect how lenders see you, so treat it like any other bill.


### How long do negative items stay on my credit report?


Most negative information stays for seven years, and bankruptcies can stay for up to 10 years,[according to the CFPB](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/how-long-does-information-stay-on-my-credit-report-en-323/) . If you’re rebuilding rather than starting fresh, see[how to increase your credit score](https://www.intuit.com/blog/innovative-thinking/financial-tips/increase-credit-score/) .
